content.thinking:
I want to write this module carefully in a single pass without testing, so I'm planning the design first: a chunky swamp troll in Blizzard/Warcraft style, with huge hands, broad shoulders, a small hunched head, and exaggerated proportions around 2.6-2.9 meters tall with long arms.

Now I'm working out the skeleton layout — placing hips, spine, chest, neck, and head joints with world coordinates to keep orientation consistent, leaning the torso forward for the hunched posture, and setting up a root joint with a spine chain branching off it.

For the head joint, I'll attach it to the end of the neck chain with a slight forward-downward direction, and add a jaw joint parented to the head. Thinking more about the troll's proportions, I want a short thick neck with the head set low and forward between the shoulders, so I'll use a short catmull-rom path with a couple of named segments to keep the chain simple but still allow a slight curve.

Now I'm working out overall body scale: hunched troll stance, hips around 1.1-1.2m, shoulders near 2.2m, head topping out near 2.6-2.7m with the mohawk pushing higher. For the legs, I'm sketching a bent, slightly digitigrade stance using two-bone IK with hip and foot targets and a forward knee bend hint, estimating the limb lengths needed to span the hip-to-foot distance.

I'm also planning the leg geometry as a smooth sweep with tapering radii from thigh to ankle, then mirroring the whole chain to the opposite side with matching joint names suffixed L/R.

Bends can be given per joint or as a single value for all joints, matching the doc's limb example. For the torso, I'll loft along the spine path from hips to chest, passing a bone list like [hips, spine] so each joint projects correctly along the path.

To avoid duplicate t-values where hips and spine1 overlap, I'll just use bone: spine directly, letting the path start at spine1's position, and add a separate pelvis shape for hips. For the troll's build, I'll go with a slight potbelly over a lean physique, fitting a sturdier swamp troll rather than a lanky Blizzard-style one, and define loft stations tracing the spine curve from belly to shoulders.

I'm defining a sequence of loft stations along the torso path, each specifying position, width, and depth to shape the belly-to-shoulder profile, then reconciling the loft path's extent with the spine chain joints so the sweep doesn't overshoot past the last tracked joint.

Now I'm planning the shoulder and upper body masses—big deltoid spheres, a trapezius hump behind the neck for that hunched troll silhouette—then setting up shoulder joints and arm proportions, with the rest pose having arms hanging outward and angled rather than straight down.

Checking arm segment lengths against distances to make sure the elbow bends naturally, then thinking through how to build the hands: a palm with finger chains per digit, roughly 10 joints per hand across four fingers and a thumb, which still stays well within the joint budget.

Writing hand geometry logic...

Using a simple x-axis side vector for finger placement. Now designing the troll head itself: elongated narrow face, prominent brow, big nose, tusks jutting from the lower jaw, long swept-back pointed ears, and a mohawk, going for a swamp troll look with teal-green-gray skin tones.

Settling on a murky olive-green skin palette with darker mottling and a paler belly, contrasted with a vivid orange-red mohawk, cream bone tusks, and leather fetish accents for that classic Warcraft saturated look. Now I'm positioning the head joint and skull geometry relative to a defined head-center coordinate.

Working out the brow ridge as angled capsule arcs over deep-set glowing yellow eyes with dark slit pupils, then shaping the hooked troll snout as a curved sweep from the bridge down to the tip.

Now I'm designing the heavy underbite jaw with curved ivory tusks sprouting from the lower jaw corners, bound with brown wrap bands, plus a pair of lower fangs, before positioning the jaw joint itself.

Shaping the jaw frustum and teeth...

Now I'm moving to the ears, planning long pointed troll-style ears that sweep back and upward by extruding an outline along the back direction.

I'm confirming the x and y axes stay perpendicular for the extrusion, then placing the ear geometry on the side of the head with a small torus ring for earrings attached near the ear tip.

Now I'm designing the mohawk as the signature feature—a thick ridge of tall, flame-like blades running from the forehead down the back of the neck and upper spine, with graduated sizes, overlapping shapes, and a root-to-tip color gradient. I'm laying out 14 blades along a curved path from the forehead point down over the hump, extruding each one with its own outline shape.

Defining blade outline shapes...

I'll avoid smoothing to sidestep corner-crossing risks, opting for 7-point outlines to get a curved look safely. For positioning, blades on the head sit on the head bone while ones trailing down the back attach to spine joints.

Working out the ridge path coordinates from forehead to nape and down over the hump, I need to map how the skull curvature and shoulder loft geometry intersect to place each point correctly along the spine.

Round caps at the loft's end would create an oversized dome poking well above the torso, so flat caps would look like an abrupt cut instead. I'll taper the final stations down to a smaller width and height to form a natural neck base before the cap closes.

I'm second-guessing whether a single loft can reliably capture the chest/shoulder/hump shape without rendering feedback, so maybe a more robust approach is combining scaled sphere primitives for the pecs, belly, shoulders, and hump on top of a simpler lofted core, all painted with the same skin material.

Switching to a flat end cap at the small final station, letting the trapezius/hump spheres overlap on top to hide the seam near the neck base. I need to remember that the loft's width/height values are full extents while the sweep radius is a half-extent, so I'll adjust accordingly along the catmull-rom path.

Checking the spine joints against the torso bone chain—B and C joint positions align reasonably with the loft stations, and the closest-point projections for the hips joint look fine for the pelvis sphere placement. For the loincloth, I'm deciding to extrude flat tattered flaps (front and back) hanging from the belt rather than lathing a full skirt, positioning the front flap between the legs starting near the belt height and hanging down.

Now I'm working out leg geometry: computing hip-to-ankle distances and thigh bend angles so the knee flexes forward correctly, using the thigh/shin segment lengths to solve for the triangle height at the knee.

I'm checking whether the hip flap overlaps with the thighs, comparing their x-widths and z-depths at hip and knee height to make sure the flap sits in front without clipping through the leg geometry.

Since perfect tuning everywhere isn't realistic, I'll settle for a moderate fit and move on to the legs: widening the stance with hip and ankle x-offsets, defining a tapered thigh radius sweep, and shaping a chunky troll-like foot with a heel block and clawed toes.

Working out foot capsule placement...

I'll simplify and make each toe a single-joint digit chain off the ankle, three per foot, keeping it cheap. Then moving to arms: shoulder position and hand target give a distance that matches planned limb lengths with a backward elbow bend, and I'm setting arm segment radii to taper from shoulder to wrist.

For embellishment, I want a shoulder mass sphere parented to the chest joint, then bone/teeth fetish details — a necklace sweeping around the neck in a leather cord, plus bracers, skull totems, and feather ornaments to match a bare-chested troll aesthetic.

Rather than trying to hand-place points precisely around the torso surface, I'll build a rough closed loop around the neck/chest and drape it onto the torso surface so it naturally conforms to the body contours.

Still working out spike placement...

For the chest pendant, I want to cast a ray from in front of the torso toward it to find the skin surface point, with a fallback fixed position if the ray misses, so the skull fetish sits flush against the body.

For the belt I'm planning crossed bones, a tiny skull, feathers, and a stick totem hanging from a loop swept around the hips, oriented along the pelvis bone's facing direction.

I'm checking whether the pelvis sphere would poke out past the torso surface near the belt height—shrinking its scale slightly keeps the width under the torso radius there so the belt reads cleanly on top.

Now I'm adding a skull-shaped buckle and brass studs spaced around the belt, using the frame-based placement so each stud's position and orientation follow the belt's path properly.

For dangling bones and feathers I'm attaching spikes at points scattered around the belt sides, and for arm cuffs I'm figuring out how to loop a ring around a forearm sweep using a chain point's tangent frame, which gives me a clean way to wrap a small loop at the right spot on the arm.

For the bracer I'll add a row of studs along the cuff loop, using small spheres or pyramids lifted slightly off the surface instead of spikes since the frame's outward direction isn't well-defined. For hair, I'm planning a mohawk with bone beads and two thin braids hanging from the nape, built as catmull sweeps down the back.

I'm checking the actual torso back geometry to position the braid path correctly, since the hump curve would push a straight ponytail off the surface — rather than fight that, I'll skip the single ponytail idea and instead give the troll two side braids/dreads hanging from behind each ear down the chest, each strung with bead rings and a bone tip.

For the skin, I'm planning a paint function combining mottled base tones with a paler belly countershade, dark warts, and moss patches on upward-facing surfaces like shoulders and the top of the head, blended with top-down highlight/shadow shading in a hand-painted style.

Still blending shading layers...

I should double-check the TypeScript types line up with my paint function signature and watch for unused variable errors since I can't run a typecheck myself. Next I need to plan SVG textures for the loincloth pattern and facial war paint decals.

For the face markings, I'm working out a position-based condition on the head region to draw cheek stripes using a sinusoid pattern, checking that the x and y coordinates fall within specific bands to create tribal-style stripes.

I'm also reconsidering texture resolution—bumping the paint atlas size up to 2048 to keep the stripes crisp given how much surface area needs painting across the model.

Now I'm tallying the distinct flat colors used across bone, leather, brass, eyes, and mouth to make sure the palette stays within the limit.

I'm defining a shared tone helper that blends a base color toward warm light at the top and cool dark at the bottom, so I can reuse painted highlight shading across leather, bone, and other materials.

I'm shading the mohawk blade with a crimson-to-orange-to-yellow gradient along its height, playing off the teal skin as a complementary color pair, and setting up a function to generate this paint per blade since each has a different height.

Now I'm tackling the tusks, blending a stained yellowish-brown base into bright ivory toward the tip using a smoothstep gradient along the sweep coordinate.

For accessories, rather than giving the troll a weapon, I'm thinking bone fetishes instead—a skull necklace, belt-hung bundles of bone, feather, and teeth, tooth bracers, a shrunken skull on a cord, tusk wraps, and maybe a back-mounted totem.

I'll simplify to a belt-hanging fetish trio plus a small skull-and-feather totem lashed to the shoulder, keeping it manageable. For feathers I'm planning a curved quill-shaped SVG texture attached via frames with lean angles so hanging feathers droop naturally from their attachment points.

I'll make two feather color variants, red-orange and teal-white, plus bone-bead ties, and scatter small moss tuft cards across the shoulders and head hump using a surface filter targeting upward-facing, elevated points.

For swamp troll styling, I'm adding hanging vines over the shoulders and a few small mushrooms on the shoulder hump — built from hemisphere caps with painted spots and cream cylinder stems, using position-based painting since the hemisphere geometry's UVs aren't reliable for texture placement.

I'm also mixing darker mud brown into the leg skin paint near the feet, scattering a handful of lighter stuck-sphere warts across the torso and arms, and adding a tuft of chin moss as hanging strand cards to round out the troll's grungy, swamp-worn look.

Now I'm working out the eye geometry: placing a glowing yellow sclera ellipsoid with a dark slit-pupil ellipsoid offset forward, calculating where the eye sits on the skull's curved surface using the ellipsoid radii to find the correct forward z-position at the given x/y offset from center.

I'm positioning a brow ridge capsule above and slightly forward of each eye to create an overhanging socket, then angling the brows so the inner ends sit lower than the outer ends for a menacing, angry expression, while checking that the brow endpoints still fall within the skull's ellipsoid surface.

Now I'm building out the rest of the facial structure: adding cheekbone spheres on either side, then shaping the muzzle as a tapered capsule extending forward and slightly down from the head center to form the maxilla and nose bridge area, setting up width and radii for a wide, flat-faced look.

For the nose itself, I'm sweeping a curved spline up and outward to create a bulbous, hooked shape, with small dark spheres marking the nostrils near the tip. For the mouth, I'm placing a lower jaw capsule beneath the muzzle, but realizing the two overlap too much and leave no visible mouth gap, so I'm shrinking the muzzle radius and repositioning the jaw capsule lower to carve out a proper mouth line between them.

I'm reconsidering giving the jaw a blockier, chunkier frustumBox shape instead of a smooth capsule, matching the sharp underbite look of a Warcraft-style troll, while checking overall head proportions against the body height to make sure the long face still fits believably on a heroic frame. I'll combine a chunky jaw frustum with a smoother chin, aiming the jaw from the joint down to the chin point, and adding a dark interior box to suggest the open mouth cavity.

Now I'm positioning the lower tusks, curving them from the jaw corner outward and upward past the muzzle so they jut forward and beside the nose, sized to roughly extend outside the muzzle width and reach about .3m in length for a dramatic troll silhouette. I'm also adding a bone-colored ring partway along each tusk, orienting it perpendicular to the tusk's curve so it reads as a wrapped band rather than lying flat.

Next I'm sketching small tooth spikes jutting down from the upper lip and up from the lower jaw, keeping an eye on the overall part budget since each tooth adds another mesh to the total count.

Placing gold hoop rings along the ear rim facing outward, then moving to the neck as a smooth tapered sweep connecting to the head positioned slightly forward.

Trapezius provides the connection. Now I'm setting up the head joint as a child of the neck chain's final joint, with a slight downward-forward orientation so the head looks naturally ahead, and assigning role labels like "head" and "neck" to keep the skeleton semantically organized.

For jaw-attached parts I'll bind to the jaw bone, and skull parts stay rigidly weighted to the head bone since they're simple smooth-skinned pieces.

Moving to arms now, I'm placing deltoid spheres at the shoulders with slight scaling for a natural shape, binding them rigidly to the first arm joint, and checking that the shoulder ball sits just inside the torso width so there's no clipping — then working out the upper arm's hang direction from shoulder toward elbow with an appropriate radius.

Checking arm reach against torso and thigh widths confirms the hands clear the body outward, but the initial hand target is too far for the arm's reach so I adjust the limb lengths and lower the hand position slightly to get a believable gorilla-like bend with knuckles hanging near knee height. I'm computing the hand's orientation vector from elbow to wrist and sizing the palm geometry accordingly, keeping the hands deliberately oversized for a troll aesthetic.

Working out finger placement...

Now I'm working out the four fingers' positions along the z-offsets with varying lengths, building each from a base point at the palm's edge, extending segments along the direction and normal vectors to curl them inward, with tapering radii toward the tips.

I'm also sketching the thumb's chain separately, starting from a point further down the wrist and angled outward, plus adding claw spikes and knuckle spheres at each finger base, making sure joint names stay unique and valid for the chain structure before tallying up all the parts.

Now I'm roughly budgeting total mesh count across the whole character: torso, pelvis, legs, feet with toes and claws, arms, shoulders, hands with fingers and knuckles, head, mohawk blades, fetish ornaments, belt, cards, mushrooms, teeth, warts, and bone ties -- landing somewhere around 350+ pieces total, checking that sweep segment counts and small sphere geometries keep the triangle budget well under 60k. For the mohawk, I'm working out the spine path along the skull's ellipsoid shape, placing blade bases from the forehead back along the top ridge.

Still plotting skull/neck coordinates...

I think I should simplify the mohawk structure instead: just run it from forehead through crown to nape with nine skull blades plus three smaller nape/hump blades, backed by a thick ridge-band sweep along the skull centerline.

Confirming the tangent stays perpendicular to the normal, so blades lean backward along that direction with tapered width and a height profile peaking near the crown and tapering toward the ends.

I'm setting a thickness taper from base to tip, coloring blades with a gradient along their outline, and defining the extrusion so the blade base embeds slightly into the surface along the normal. I'm also considering adding a second row of smaller offset blades behind the main row for extra fullness.

I think I'll double up the mohawk blades with a staggered second layer at reduced height and lateral offset, bringing the total to around 27 blades plus the nape ones for roughly 35 parts. I'm also sketching in two gold rings and a couple of dark red braids hanging from the mohawk for extra detail.

For the braids, I'm planning a zigzag banded coloring pattern based on position, with cylindrical bead rings along the strand and a bone fang tassel at the tip. Now I'm listing out the imports I'll need for the TypeScript build—mesh merging utilities, the builder and frame helpers, limb IK, randomness, path curves, and various procedural texture functions like paint, noise, and mottle—making sure only what's actually used gets imported.

I'm sorting out the typing nuances for the geometry merge function, deciding to add a null check and throw if the merge fails even if the types suggest it's non-nullable, just to be safe. Then I'm setting up small vector helpers and confirming how frame() and the texture/svg functions will be called for the card meshes.

Now I'm starting to lay out the metadata object and the color palette constants, like a bone tone, before building out each visual feature in code.

Still writing color constants...

Adding muddy feet, mossy top surfaces, and wart cell patterns...

Still writing war paint logic...

I should also check whether tusks or nose regions overlap this striping and exclude them, then move on to a chest tattoo with concentric tribal lines centered around a point on the torso.

Now I'm shaping that tattoo into chevron stripes using a distance function combining y and |x|, bounded to a chest region with proper normal facing outward, while deciding to skip any arm tattoo bands for now.

Next I'm setting up a leather material with a base brown tone and a mottled wear pattern using noise, wrapping it in a reusable `tone()` helper function for generating paints from color inputs.

For the loincloth, I'm working through how to render a tribal-patterned leather flap since extruded geometry only accepts paints, not textures. I'm leaning toward building it from double-sided cards attached at the hip, hanging downward with a tattered-edge texture, since cards support textured surfaces and can be shaded naturally by their frame orientation—planning separate front and back flaps plus side strips, all textured with leather and tribal stitching.

Now I'm reasoning through the card's orientation: since the hanging geometry flips the artwork upside-down when viewed from the front, I need to author the SVG inverted—placing the hem detail at the top and the attach edge at the bottom—so I'll wrap the upright artwork in a 180-degree rotation transform to correct for this.

For the back flap I'll flip its flow direction to [0,0,-1] so it's correctly oriented when seen from behind, and I confirm the card plane aligns with width and length axes so the front faces forward properly. Next I'm planning additional SVG elements: feathers, moss strands, and possibly a bone-rune texture for a skull pendant's painted plates.

For the fetish layout, I'm sketching out the full set: a draped necklace with bone/fang pendants and a central skull, a belt with a skull buckle and studs carrying bundles of bones, feathers, and pouches at the hips, bone-spiked bracers on the forearms, bone spike rings and feather clusters at the shoulders, and gold-wrapped tusks with ear decorations.

Now I'm designing a reusable skull-building helper that constructs a cranium, cheeks, eye sockets, nose cavity, and jaw from primitive shapes, oriented using a quaternion computed from a facing direction so each skull decoration can be placed and rotated correctly on the body.

Still working out skull proportions...

I'm defining the nose hole and teeth as small dark and light boxes on the face, then sketching a bone helper that builds a cartoon bone shape from a shaft capsule with knob spheres at each end.

Setting up imports and starting the build function...

Writing feather SVG texture...

I need to check the stroke width scales properly at the final render size, and think about orientation — the feather needs to be flipped for hanging cards so the quill points up instead of down.

Deciding to only use hanging feathers for belt, necklace, braid ends, and standing ones for the shoulder fetish, with a hang parameter controlling rotation. For moss I'll just always use the hanging convention since all the strands drape downward from chin, shoulders, and hump.

Now I'm thinking through where to scatter moss clumps — filtering surface hits by upward-facing normals and height on the torso top and hump sphere, using frames oriented along the up vector since moss sits on flat-ish top surfaces rather than hanging.

For mushrooms, I'm planning to shoot rays downward at shoulder hump positions to find skin hits, then build a tiny stem-and-cap mesh attached to each hit point offset slightly along the surface normal.

Confirming hit.axis works as the facing unit vector for direction input, so I'll define a mush(hit, s) helper. For the cap paint I'm adding reddish-orange spots on cream with small size and moderate density, tuning the texel scale so spots read clearly at the mushroom's tiny cap size.

Now I'm figuring out how to add spiky dorsal ridges along a swamp troll's back using a sweep along the torso — placing bone-colored spikes at regular intervals, using angle 0 to target the back-facing side of the vertical tube, and confirming the spike function takes a base frame and axis-aligned tip length per the sweep API.

Then I'm moving to legs and feet: writing code that loops over left/right sides, computes hip, knee, and ankle points via a limb helper, and builds a chain for each leg parented to the hips joint with named sub-joints and a foot contact point. I'm checking that the chain options accept a point array for the path and a parent reference, and confirming the contact field and parenting logic line up with how the hips joint is oriented.

Next I sweep each leg with a tapering radius array for a smooth skin-colored limb, grab the ankle as the last joint in the chain, and consider adding a knee-cap sphere, scar detail, and a leather ankle cuff using a torus positioned along the leg's chain point.

Positioning the ankle ring...

Actually, I'll switch to surface loops for the cuffs instead, sweeping along the leg at a given t with a lift offset so it conforms regardless of radius — wrapping this in a reusable helper that generates the path and stud placements. Then I'm sketching the arm sweep and the foot capsule geometry.

Checking the foot capsule tapers: with tapered radii at the ankle and toe ends, the bottom sits about 1% below ground, which is close enough to flat. Then I'm working out toe joint placement, parenting each toe to the ankle and spacing them with a small lateral offset per toe index.

Each toe gets a tapered capsule for its digit shape and a spike positioned at the tip for the claw, angled slightly forward-down so it reads naturally. I'm double-checking the joint uses aim-at-tip orientation and that the big toe is slightly thicker than the others.

For the arm, I'm sweeping a capsule chain through shoulder, elbow, and wrist points parented to the chest joint, then adding a spike at the elbow to suggest a bony protrusion — positioning its base slightly behind the joint so it clears the arm's radius.

I'm giving it asymmetric shoulder detailing: the right shoulder gets a cluster of three bone spikes fanning outward from the deltoid at varied angles, while the left shoulder instead gets moss, mushrooms, and feather growths for visual contrast.

Now I'm working out the head's coordinate frame, defining a relative point helper centered on the head position, then placing the head and jaw joints with specific offsets and forward-aiming directions before moving into attaching individual head features.

I'm detailing facial parts — a sphere skull, then brow geometry defined as capsule shapes going from inner to outer points with specific radii, shaping an angry-looking brow where the inner edge sits lower than the outer, sloping down toward the nose.

I'm placing a brow ridge sphere above the eyes, then sizing the sclera spheres so the brow slightly overlaps the eye tops, creating a hooded look, and positioning a small dark pupil slit that pokes forward out of the sclera toward the front of the face.

Now I'm adding a glowing eye part scaled uniformly, cheekbone spheres, and shaping the muzzle as a capsule with tapered radii, adjusting its center and radius so the top-lip bottom lands around the right height.

Then I'm defining the jaw as a frustum box tube spanning along the forward axis, sizing its width and height so the top aligns with the muzzle bottom and checking for an underbite where the jaw extends further forward than the muzzle tip.

I should add a chunky chin ridge and a lower lip detail for the jaw. For the mouth interior, I'm considering a dark box placed between the muzzle bottom and jaw top, but that gap is nearly closed at rest, so I may need to pose the jaw slightly open to reveal it.

I need to pose the jaw joint with a forward-tilting rotation to open the mouth, but this must happen after all jaw parts are built, since the placement coordinates assume rest pose and posing first would misplace them relative to world space.

Checking the geometry: with the jaw pivot behind, opening 14° creates roughly a 0.1m gap at the front, which works well with the tongue sitting on the jaw and the tusks tipping down slightly while still clearing upward overall. Now I'm moving on to sweeping the nose shape with a curve through several control points.

Shaping the tusk radius...

I'm placing the nostrils as small dark spheres tucked under the nose tip, then adding a gold septum ring hanging below between them, oriented so its torus axis runs along the X direction.

Now I'm positioning the ears, and sketching warts along the brow and upper lip as small stick shapes. For teeth, I'm arranging eight small cones around the muzzle's lower arc for the upper row, pointing downward with tapering positions toward the front, and planning a matching upward-pointing set along the jaw top for the lower teeth.

Placing more teeth...

Checking that lower teeth stay merged with the jaw bone and confirming the tusks and tongue placement -- the tongue as a flattened scaled sphere inside the jaw, and tusks sprouting from the jaw corners with control points bending outward and up, though I'm double-checking the tusk curve doesn't poke through the jaw front.

Working on tusk geometry -- I'm checking whether a second smaller tusk pair would collide with the muzzle front and deciding to skip it, then adding gold band rings along the main tusks by sampling points on the sweep curve and computing ring radii that taper with the tusk's shrinking profile.

Next I'm planning the mohawk, braids trailing from behind each ear, and chin moss/hair, all tied to the head bone.

Now adding a chin moss tuft using manually placed card frames bound to the jaw bone, hanging downward with a green gradient texture. Writing SVG texture code...

I realize I should author the drawing upright as it should finally appear—attached at top, free end at bottom—then wrap it in a 180-degree rotation to correct the orientation since the card displays upside-down downstream.

Writing moss strand path...

For the torso I'm planning to use a loft operation along the spine bone with skin coloring, round start cap and flat end cap, checking that the sweep options support a "sides" parameter for segment count.

Now I'm sketching chest and belly details — adding pec spheres flattened and positioned near the chest bone, and considering whether to add a separate pot-belly sphere or just adjust the torso loft's belly station to bulge outward instead.

Adjusting the spine station positions and widths to shape the torso profile, shifting the belly station forward in z while tweaking width and height at each height level to get a natural silhouette, then checking that shoulder ball placement still fits within the chest width and that the spine chain and neck path connect smoothly into the torso's top.

Now I'm placing the neck segments and verifying the head joint lands near the top of the neck, then adjusting neck radii to keep it proportionally thick but not wider than the head. I'm also positioning the hump sphere, trapezius capsules, and deltoid spheres relative to the spine tip and shoulder joints, confirming the shoulder joint location matches the arm chain's first point before moving on to attachment points for wrists and other fetish accessories like the necklace.

Working out a draped closed path for the necklace around the neck using catmull-rom points, but I'm second-guessing whether some of those points land inside the torso mesh rather than on its surface, since the drape function will snap them to the nearest surface which could be the neck cap instead of the chest front.

I'm reconsidering the approach entirely -- rather than draping points near the torso, it's cleaner to build an explicit closed loop (like an ellipse) positioned just outside the neck/shoulder geometry, since the trapezius capsules and hump shapes complicate where the true surface sits in that region.

Good, so I'll target the torso, hump, and trap/pec parts as surfaces for the necklace, placing points around the neck base at radius .32 with a V-shaped sag in front, imagining it as a heavy ring of large beads like fangs or bones.

I'm deciding to build a cord with large ivory fangs hanging from the front half, plus a skull pendant. I'll iterate along the closed drape path, checking each point's z-position to identify the front half, and spawn downward-pointing spike shapes for fangs angled slightly outward, with roughly 9 of 18 points qualifying as front-facing. For the skull pendant, I'm working out how to find the lowest front-center point on the torso surface to anchor it.

Confirming that ray hits the torso front at y1.78, good. Now I'm figuring out belt placement around y1.2 where the torso cross-section is roughly .68 wide and .6 deep, sweeping a leather loop with slight lift to sit naturally on the surface.

Thinking through the belt geometry more -- rather than a complex box section, I'll simplify to two parallel circular sweeps (a wider belt plus a thinner strap) at slightly offset heights, which avoids ambiguity around sweep orientation and binormal axes.

I'm placing a gold buckle plate at the front of the loop using a ray hit test, with a small ivory skull emblem mounted on it facing forward. For the belt path itself, I'm confirming the loop starts at world +Z (front) when the direction vector points up, so I can reliably position decorative studs and fetishes at normalized positions along the closed path using frame sampling.

For the hanging ornaments I'm finding points along the belt by locating the closest parameter on the path near each hip and back position, then using those points to hang items: a crossed bone pair and feather cards with a small skull on the left hip, a leather pouch with a fang cluster and shrunken-head totem on the right hip, and a trailing cluster of feather cards at the back.

These hanging pieces should rig to the hips/root bone so they stay rigid rather than deforming with the belt weights. For the loincloth, I'm checking that the front flap, attached near the hip area, clears the thigh geometry -- comparing the flap's z-depth against the thigh's front edge to make sure it hangs just outside the leg volume rather than intersecting it.

Since the thigh pushes forward toward the knee, a straight-down flap would collide with the knee by the time it reaches that height. I'm tilting the card using a lean angle around 150-160 degrees so the bottom swings forward in sync with the leg's natural curve, clearing the knee front by roughly the right margin.

For the loincloth itself I'm sketching a leather texture with a jagged, stitched hem, a belt band at the top, and a diamond stitch pattern down the center, designing it to attach upright before being rotated into place. Writing SVG path code...

Now I'm moving on to arm cuffs and bracers with bone studs.

Skipping that, I'm thinking through the ankle detailing: loops need to sit on the leg sweep surface, then adding an ankle band with hanging ivory fangs spaced around it using the same spike-placement approach as before.

For the rest, I'm keeping scope tight -- skipping wrist wrap fetishes, extra elbow details, and rune markings to avoid bloating part count. I am considering adding a small bone-feather totem bundle on the left shoulder: a leaning wooden pole topped with a tiny skull and a few hanging feather cards, though that might push the height too far and I should weigh whether it's worth including.

Checking total figure height against the mohawk hair peak to keep the troll's silhouette proportional, then settling on anchoring the fetish pole directly into the shoulder's deltoid geometry so it reads as lashed-on rather than floating. I'm also sketching where to scatter a few small mushrooms and moss across the back hump for texture.
